steps.body:
Two events are **independent** when learning one leaves the other's probability exactly where it was:

P(A | B) = P(A).

A card's suit and its rank are like this. P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13. Told the card is a heart, the world shrinks to 13 cards — but exactly one is a king, so it is still 1/13.
You are told the card is a heart. Thirteen cards survive.

widget.prompt: Shade the kings among the 13 surviving hearts — that fraction is P(king | heart).
widget.successFeedback: 1 of 13 — the same 1/13 as before the condition. Suit carried no information about rank, so the number did not budge.
widget.lowFeedback: There is exactly one king of hearts among the 13 hearts. Shade it.
widget.highFeedback: Only one heart is a king. Shading four would count the kings of every suit, but three of those were ruled out by the condition.

predict.prompt: You'll shade 1/13 of the grid. Will that cover more or less than half of it?
predict.reveal: Half means the numerator is half the denominator — 6.5/13 here — and 1 is less. Probability as shaded area makes the benchmark visible before you count a single cell.

cml.actionGoal: Select regions of an equal-outcome sample space and coordinate area with event probability.

explanationVariants: P(king) = 1/13 and P(king | heart) = 1/13. The condition changed nothing, so suit and rank are independent.
The heart row is a faithful miniature of the whole deck: same mix of ranks, just 13 cards instead of 52.

widget.prompt: P(king) = 1/13 and P(king | heart) = 1/13. What does that tell you?

options.label: Suit and rank are independent — knowing the suit tells you nothing about the rank.
options.feedback: Right — the defining test is whether the condition moves the probability. Here it does not.

options.label: Kings and hearts are mutually exclusive.
options.feedback: The king of hearts is both at once, so the events certainly can co-occur. Exclusive would mean P(king and heart) = 0.

options.label: P(king and heart) = 0.
options.feedback: That card exists: P(king and heart) = 1/52. Independence says the joint equals 1/4 × 1/13, which is exactly 1/52.

options.label: Every heart is equally likely to be a king.
options.feedback: That sentence is about one card being a king or not, and it is not what independence compares. Independence compares P(king) with P(king | heart).

explanationVariants: P(sport) = 0.55 across the school, but P(sport | bus) = 0.40. The condition moved the number, so the events are dependent.
Bus riders play sports at a lower rate than the school as a whole — that difference IS the dependence.

widget.prompt: For the 200 students: P(sport) = 0.55 and P(sport | bus) = 0.40. Are travel and sport independent?

options.label: Dependent — knowing they take the bus changes the sport probability.
options.feedback: Right — 0.40 ≠ 0.55, so the condition carried real information.

options.label: Independent — both numbers are between 0 and 1.
options.feedback: Every probability is between 0 and 1, so that can never distinguish the two cases. The test is whether conditioning moves the number.

options.label: Independent — 40% and 55% are both fairly common outcomes.
options.feedback: Independence is not about the sizes being similar; it is about them being *equal*. A 15-point gap means the bus tells you something.

options.label: Impossible to say without knowing P(bus).
options.feedback: P(A | B) versus P(A) is already the whole test. P(bus) would be needed only for the product form of the same check.

steps.body:
Independence is **symmetric**. If B tells you nothing about A, then A tells you nothing about B:

P(A | B) = P(A)  ⟺  P(B | A) = P(B).

So you may test whichever direction is easier. Careful: independence is a claim about *information*, not about causation, and it must be checked — never assumed because two things "feel unrelated".

explanationVariants: P(heart | king) = 1/4, and P(heart) = 13/52 = 1/4. Same number, so the symmetry holds.
One of the four kings is a heart, and one of the four suits is hearts — the condition again changes nothing.

widget.prompt: A card is drawn and you are told it is a **king**. Find P(heart | king) as a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 4/52, the unconditional P(king). The question asks about the suit given the rank, so the four kings are the world: one is a heart.
That would mean half the kings are hearts. There are four kings, one per suit, so it is 1 of 4.
That is 1/52, the joint P(king and heart). Conditioning on king divides that by P(king) = 4/52, giving 1/4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: One of the 4 kings is a heart: 1/4 = 0.25, exactly P(heart). Independence again.

explanationVariants: Ask whether learning the first event would move your estimate of the second. If it would, they are dependent.
Physical separation is a good clue, but it is not proof — the real test is whether P(A | B) equals P(A).

widget.prompt: Would knowing the first event change the chance of the second?

items.label: Flip 1 is heads · flip 2 is heads
items.feedback: The coin has no memory. P(heads on flip 2) is 1/2 whatever flip 1 did.

items.label: First card is an ace · second card is an ace (no replacement)
items.feedback: Removing an ace leaves 3 aces in 51 cards, so the second probability drops from 4/52 to 3/51. The draw changed the deck.

items.label: The card is a heart · the card is a king
items.feedback: One of the 13 hearts is a king, and one of every 13 cards is a king. The suit carries no rank information.

items.label: It rained today · the roads are wet
items.feedback: Rain sharply raises the chance of wet roads, so knowing one moves the other a long way.

widget.missFeedback: For each pair, ask: after learning the first, would you revise your estimate of the second?
widget.successFeedback: Coins and card-suits carry no information across; a shrinking deck and a rainy sky carry plenty.

hints: You have P(A ∩ B) and P(B). That is enough to build P(A | B).
Compare your answer with P(A) = 0.40. If they match, the events are independent.
explanationVariants: P(A | B) = 0.10/0.25 = 0.40, which equals P(A). The events are independent — the condition moved nothing.
Check the product instead: P(A) × P(B) = 0.40 × 0.25 = 0.10, exactly the given joint. Same verdict.

commonErrors.feedback: That is P(B), the condition itself. You want the share of B that is also A: 0.10 divided by 0.25.
That is the joint P(A ∩ B). A conditional divides it by P(B), which enlarges it to 0.40.
That is 0.40 + 0.25. Conditioning is a ratio, never a sum — and a probability of 0.65 for A given B would need justifying, not adding.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 0.10/0.25 = 0.40 = P(A), so A and B are independent.

steps.body: Independence means the condition does nothing.
takeaways: A and B are independent when P(A | B) = P(A) — learning B moves nothing.
The relation is symmetric: test whichever direction has the easier numbers.
Independence must be checked against the numbers; "they seem unrelated" is not evidence.
steps.teaser: Next: a one-line product test that settles it without any conditioning at all.

concept.body: Ask one question: *does the news change my estimate?* If P(A) was 0.3 before you heard about B and it is still 0.3 after, B was worthless news and the events are independent. If it moves at all — up or down — they are dependent.

explanationVariants: P(rain) = 0.20 but P(rain | cloudy) = 0.60. The condition tripled it, so the events are dependent.
Any change at all — even a small one — means the events carry information about each other.

widget.prompt: P(rain) = 0.20 and P(rain | cloudy morning) = 0.60. Independent or dependent?

options.label: Dependent
options.feedback: Right — the condition moved the probability from 0.20 to 0.60, so the cloudy morning was informative.

options.label: Independent
options.feedback: Independence would require P(rain | cloudy) to still be 0.20. It tripled instead.
